utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before Your Honours entered the courtroom, the accused were photographed. We had not been informed who was the person who photographed them, for what reasons, and who authorised taking those photographs. We think it was completely unauthorised, or somebody should have informed us what it was all about, and I believe that our authorisation should have also been sought, or at least our opinion should have been sought on this photography. So we should like to propose that the film be seized, that the photographer be intercepted and his film be seized. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic, it is for the Trial Chamber to decide whether or not to authorise taking of photographs, and today these photographers were indeed authorised by the Trial Chamber. This is a public trial, and we normally give the authorisation to photographers to take a few pictures, normally before the beginning of a trial. All right, so I think -- yes, Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I accept your explanation that it is the Chamber which authorises such photography, but I believe we should be notified in advance that this is going to take place and to also know that the Chamber has issued such an authorisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree; I think you're right. And I actually thought, when they sought authorisation, that they would take photographs while we were here in court, just a few seconds before we would start with trial proceedings, so I, myself, was a bit taken by surprise. But we will duly notify you in the future if there any similar request is made by photographers. Let us now, before we resume with the witness, Mr. Katava, discuss briefly the question of the schedule for this week. We have noticed that once again, changes have been made in the list of witnesses. This is fine with us, except for the fact that we can't provide interpreters for Mr. Groenwald on Friday, so we would like to request Counsel Pavkovic to bring forward Mr. Groenwald to the 7th, tomorrow. We see from the letter filed by Counsel Pavkovic that Mr. Groenwald cannot testify today. I assume he can do so tomorrow, and tomorrow we will have interpreters available. No interpreters will be available on Friday, so therefore we have to bring him forward tomorrow. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The schedule for the week was not drawn up, really, to meet all the wishes of the Defence; it was dictated by the circumstances. Mr. Groenwald, who was scheduled for tomorrow, cannot, simply cannot make it tomorrow. He cannot come because he has some other business, and we had to accept to do whatever to meet his wishes and his availability, and he said that he would be available on Friday only. As for the schedule that we have now, the witness Kolk will not be coming. At the very last moment, when we finished the list, we received a cable that she did not want to testify, that she refused to testify. She was scheduled for the 7th of July; that is, on Wednesday, or rather tomorrow. These are the circumstances which made us make the schedule, draw up the schedule that you received today. I really do not know what else we can do. We hoped, and we really did our best, to go by the original schedule, but there were some circumstances beyond our power. We really insisted with the gentleman to come and appear before the Court tomorrow, and he said no, he would be available only on Friday. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: First of all, let me point out that the Tribunal, knowing that one or two people, Dutch-speaking people, would come today and tomorrow, have already made provision for three interpreters, and we will incur the necessary expenses, so they will be available whether or not we use them, whereas they are not available on Friday. On Friday there will be no interpretation from Dutch into English and Bosnian-Croatian, and vice versa. First point. Second point, we wonder what sort of business Mr. Groenwald is involved in. If he is summoned by the Court, he should come over tomorrow. Has he got any urgent business that he can't just cast aside for the sake of testifying here before the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Groenwald is the principal of a school, and we accepted the reasons he said. He said he could not really come; he would not be available. We wanted him to come when it would suit best the Defence in view of the kind of examination that we intended to conduct, but he said that he would be available on Friday only. But Mr. Groenwald does speak English, so perhaps this might be of some significance, of some importance, if we are discussing interpreters. Perhaps that is important. And as for the lady witness for whom Dutch interpreters have been provided for today and tomorrow, on the 1st of July, the time when we had drawn up the list, it was only after that we received a fax informing us that she was now refusing to testify. Her case is not all that important. But if Mr. Groenwald is willing to speak English, then we shall not be needing other interpreters on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, allow me to just make a remark. I hereby refer to the summary of Mr. Groenwald's testify. If he is to repeat in front of you what is supposed to be in his summary, there is no problem whatsoever. We do agree to what is being said in the summary of his testimony. Since his testimony is not going to be challenged, or hardly so, I think that he could testify in English. Because we know that Dutch people are very gifted for languages, and since he is going to be a short witness, it is going to be a short testimony, unchallenged testimony, he could easily testify in English. Allow me to make another observation regarding the following weeks, next week and the one after. We still don't know for sure whether some or all accused are going to testify or not. Today, since we have to prepare for such possibilities, we should know about it. I believe that the witnesses summoned by Counsel Pavkovic should have finished, if not by the end of this week, towards the middle of next week. We are going to have an ethnologist, a Norwegian ethnologist, next week; but after him or her, I think it is up to the accused to testify if they wish. But we should know today, as soon as we can. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So as for Mr. Groenwald, we could call him on Friday on the assumption that he will be speaking in English, and as the Prosecutor just pointed out, his testimony will most likely be brief. Let me now turn to the point made by the Prosecutor. We agree with the Prosecutor; I think it is high time for us to know the programme for the next two weeks. Are you now in a position to tell us if and when the accused will testify, will give evidence as witnesses, and which accused, and when, so that the Prosecutor may prepare?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know, Mr. President. Do you mean only my client, or does this question include all the accused? I do not know, really. As for my client, I will know only at the end of the week, after we have heard all the witnesses, because you see, we have now one witness cancelling her appearance, and we just do not know. I hope that all the witnesses that you have on your list will appear before the Court and give their evidence, and that I shall also be able to complete my part by the end of this week, unless, of course, the Prosecution has more questions than envisaged by us beforehand. I need to seize this opportunity to thank Mr. Terrier for being so understanding, and I assure him that Mr. Groenwald will testify as Mr. Terrier has pointed out: That is, succinctly, shortly, and, I believe, with regard to circumstances which do not raise any particular questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I do understand your position with regard to your client, but I wonder whether the other Defence counsel are in a position to let us know whether or not they intend to call the accused. I'm thinking in particular of Counsel Radovic or Slokovic-Glumac. I wonder whether they have already decided whether or not to call the accused. Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, as for the two of us or, rather, our two clients, they will give evidence. Zoran Kupreskic will be a witness in his own case and in the case against his brother, so that both my colleague Slokovic-Glumac and I will be examining them. Mirjan Kupreskic, likewise he will testify both in his case and in the case against his brother, so that they will be examined by both of us, that is, Ms. Slokovic-Glumac and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Ms. Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should merely like to add something with regard to the schedule. Of course, the Prosecution is fully entitled to know how we envisaged this last week of the Defence case. I presume that we shall have to call yet another witness, at least one witness more, in view of the list which was submitted to us during the Defence case, which we believe are of some weight. Now, we are referring to the list of HDZ members and a list that was submitted yesterday or, rather, the text which was tendered into evidence by the Prosecution, and that is the alleged list of HDZ members. So these are the two documents which were submitted at a later date in the course of the Defence case, and we shall have to call a witness. I hope that you will allow us not to prepare a summary, because we have to talk to that person who compiled those lists. We have not talked yet to this person. We have yet to ascertain that this person is quite conversant with all the details about how these lists were compiled, so that next week, after we acknowledge this testimony, we should like to call that witness, and we shall also have some more documents to tender into evidence. Only after that, we will call our clients to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do I understand you would be prepared to call Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic as witnesses next week, probably the middle of next week, after calling the witness you just mentioned? All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: There will be yet another problem, but I believe we shall be able to solve it towards the end of the week when we prepare some documents. We believe that some documents which have not yet been admitted into evidence, the Court deemed them not to be of vital importance, but we do think they are indeed of major importance, and we shall submit additional documentation to support our claim. We also believe that the testimony of Zoran and Mirjan will depend on whether the Court will admit these documents. Of course we shall provide our reasons for which we insist, once again, that those documents be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We shall call our client, the accused Vlatko Kupreskic, to give evidence after the testimony of the first and the second accused. Thank you. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have not yet decided on this matter, but as things stand now, I do not think that Drago Josipovic will be giving his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Dragan Papic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have not yet decided either, but we shall inform the Court in a few days' time. As I was informed yesterday during my visit at the detention unit, Dragan Papic has some health problems, health complaints. He is scheduled for a surgical intervention next week on his nose. He shall report to the hospital on the 14th, and the surgery would take place on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Now, the last point, the point raised by Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, I wonder whether the Prosecutor will be prepared to dispense with the statement by the witness Counsel Slokovic-Glumac is proposing to call next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We won't have any objection on this point. However, Your Honour, we would like to be informed of the documents that are going to be used, not of the arguments, as such, but that we should know which documents are going to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We're grateful to the Prosecutor for accepting that the witness will be called without any document being handed over in advance to the Prosecutor. I think it's the Prosecutor's request that the documents should be shown to the Prosecutor in advance. Whether it is acceptable, I think it is quite sensible. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, would you be prepared to hand over to the Prosecutor those documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not think we shall have any other documents. It is simply the person who was doing these lists. It is the Prosecution Exhibit 535 and the other one which was admitted yesterday. I do not know which number it was. I think it was P371. So we are calling the witness who compiled those lists, and we are calling this person to make an analysis of the lists and who will give us the reasons for which these lists were compiled, and if any documentation needs to be presented alongside these documents, we shall try to find those documents. But we shall also urge the witness to come to The Hague next week, and of course we shall hand over to the Prosecution all the relevant details, who that person is, where he or she works, since when, and so on and so forth so they can verify it all. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Before we resume with the testimony of Mr. Katava, on behalf of the Court, I would like to make two points. First of all, we understand that Mr. Dragan Papic will undergo surgery next week. I mean we assume that we will proceed even in his absence, because we can't give leave to be absent from court, but our trial proceedings will go on in his absence because his Defence counsel will be here. Then, of course, if he recovers, he could always give evidence towards the end of the month, before we end our proceedings on the 23rd of July. So this is the basic assumption. If there are no other matters to be discussed, we can resume with the testimony of Mr. Katava. Mr. Katava, thank you so much for being patient. Counsel Pavkovic, would you like to resume your examination in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Katava.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you rested?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So we can proceed?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we should now go into n.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. All right, we'll go into private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, yesterday you said that you had got to know Drago Josipovic only in 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And that was when the indictment was confirmed and published. Do you know whether Drago Josipovic was active in political work in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he and politics, that just doesn't go together. I think that he is very naive politically. He worked in large company which employed over 3.000 people. I think he didn't care about politics. But I didn't know him -- his wife was active politically, but I hope he will not be offended if I say that he knew nothing about politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he could have participated in the making of any military or civilian decisions in the Vitez municipality in the same period?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, there's no question of that. If he took part in any decision making, he would only have done so in the self-management bodies in the company in which he worked. That was all he was capable of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: General Blaskic, in his statement, mentioned a meeting which was held on the 15th of April, 1993, at 22.30 hours, which was allegedly attended by Nikola Krizanovic, as far as I can remember, Pero Skopljak, Ivica Santic, and Tihomir Blaskic. Do you know anything about the content of that meeting? Because these witnesses were called but did not come to the Court, except for General Tihomir Blaskic. In the indictment, it says, among other things, that the accused -- and I'm only asking you about Drago Josipovic -- took part in military training, and that they armed themselves, evacuated civilian Bosnian Croats the night before the attack, organised HVO soldiers, weapons, ammunition, and other things. Can you say whether these are persons who could have carried out the planning and organising, as the indictment says, of the attack on Ahmici, if this was done systematically?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, but professionally?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I knew this man for a very brief period of time under conditions which were not conducive to establishing friendships. I am not a psychologist by profession, and in the year during which I knew him before he came here to the detention unit, I cannot evaluate whether he could have done that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You testified today, and yesterday, too, you said you were interviewed by the Prosecution on the 16th of December, '97; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you testify today and yesterday in the same manner as in the statement that you made to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, these -- yes, my statements should be identical, 100 per cent. Both then and yesterday and today, I have been telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But was it only on the 16th of April, 1993, that you were asked --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't mean the interview you gave on the 16th of April, but about the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, only about that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Because you were also in the indictment, which was subsequently changed for a number of other accused, for a longer period of time, not only on that particular date, and that is why I asked you that. But just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Will you please show P371 to the witness. My learned friend Pavkovic wants to say something, and I call upon him to say it publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at page 74, Number 53. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The number, you said?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you if you were an HDZ member.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean page 74, Number 53.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I've found my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us, what is the title of that document?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Members of the Organised Resistance."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How is it that your name figures there if you are not a member of the HDZ, as you've told us?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not think that this has anything to do with the HDZ, because from what I can see here, this list, only names of men are featured in this list, and there are a number of women who are members of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that there were women who were HDZ members?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and yet I do not see any female name on this list, particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, how is it possible that in P353, where shares were distributed and where women were also mentioned as members of the HVO, and here they do not figure?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Here, next to my name, my personal numbers are right and other data are correct, but I'm afraid that this is not my signature. Somebody else signed it in my name. This is not my signature. All I can-- about -- I'm sorry, I didn't get your last question. What was it? It had to do something with shares.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a smaller, shorter list involving a lesser number of persons than the number of persons found in 353, where we also have women figuring as members of the HVO. Why is it that they are not on this list and they are on that other list?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I believe this was simply a matter of political attitude of Croats and Muslims who were at war. And in the end, the High Representative for Bosnia, Mr. Westendorp, decided that these papers, called certificates or state bonds, were distributed among people who took part in the war who were receiving no salaries, and they were also.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were 9 billion claimed by the B and H, and he brought it down to 7 billion; I do not know whether they are dollars or marks. And then everybody claimed something, and this is a kind of state property which is still only on paper, and it was decided by him to distribute it on the basis of -- I don't know what kind of ratio; 75/25, or whatever per cent. This was, again, a decision of the High Representative, because representatives of Bosniaks and Muslims could not agree on the distribution, so he decided on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, but my question was, why is this list of persons in '92 -- or rather '91 to '92 -- shorter than the list compiled subsequently? I did already mention the number of the exhibit which also shows that women were also members of the HVO. Why is it that in this list we have a lesser number of persons than in the shares list?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Why is that list longer than this one? Well, you will have to ask the authors of that list. It is my guess that this paper, this list, includes only able-bodied men, and when it came to the list for shareholders, then they tried to cover as many people as possible. And it had nothing to do with able-bodied people of military age; it was simply distributed over a much wider number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac also for cross-examination? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Only a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Katava. Only a couple of questions. You told us, with reference to the indictment which was confirmed by this Tribunal, that you learned of it in 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it was the end of 1996 or early 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But would you know, or could you be more accurate? Was it '96, or '97?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it was the end of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And did you take any steps after you learned about the indictment? Did you try to do something?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, a certain period of time had to pass, because at first, only the indictment had been publicised, and one had to learn what was one charged for directly. It was a very hard time for me psychologically. After I had read all the counts of the indictment confirmed by this Tribunal, I was greatly relieved because I knew the things I was being charged for I had not done, and it was subsequently confirmed by the Tribunal that I was not the person present there. So a group of people on the accused under that indictment, that is seven of us, and I'm saying this, I'm using the word "fate"; I don't know how it will be translated or interpreted. Fate has brought us together, because the living conditions were extremely hard, and there is no need to explain to you that international arrest warrants had been issued, that everybody could arrest us, anybody who would bring us into custody, and both we or members of our families could perish in such an attempt. So during that period of time, which was very difficult, mentally, psychologically, for me, each and every one of us sought some remedy, sought some kind of therapy. Yet sometime in the former half of 1997, we decided to put an end to our hiding and to our silence. We knew that all roads led to this courtroom, that all our paths led to this courtroom, and that there was no other road but this one. We then decided to try to somehow raise the awareness of the world barons, as we call it in Bosnia, to somehow turn to the mighty of this world to help us to collect evidence, to appear before the Court of our own free will, and thus get rid of that burden.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Katava, just a moment. Could you please tell us what people are you talking about? It was you and other people who are on a different indictment, that is, people who are indicted here, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. With all of them -- well, not on a daily basis, but we spoke, we communicated every day, except for Vlado Santic, who was not in Vitez at the time. All the others were physically present in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Right. And then you decided -- so it was the former half of 1997 you decided to take some steps to do something so as to surrender to the Tribunal in The Hague, so what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: We awaited Mr. Steiner's visit in Vitez. At the time, Mr. Steiner was the deputy of the High Representative for B and H, Mr. Carl Bildt, and we wanted to give to him, to present to him a short letter that we had written in which we were requesting, in his official capacity, begging him to try to ensure for us a fair and expeditious trial. And we insisted on this "fair and expeditious" because the proceedings against General Blaskic had already begun, and in view of the pace, of the very slow pace, we were afraid that we would be detained in custody for years. We were not afraid of anything else. We were not afraid of the final judgement; rest assured about that. That was my attitude and everybody's. We were not afraid of the final judgement, but we were afraid -- we really were afraid of the time, of the cost in time, not to mention the health, not to mention all the ways in which it would affect our families and everybody else. And with this intent in mind, we wrote a letter of similar contents to Mrs. Albright, to Mr. Sergei Labrov, the then-president of the Security Council, members of the BH presidency, believing that we were still entitled, even if accused, that we were entitled to approach the collective president of the head of the State of which we were nationals to do whatever he could at the level of the State. We also wrote to the members of the municipal assembly in Vitez, who had been elected lawfully at the last elections, and who knew all seven of us. We asked that municipal body -- and that was the legislative body of the municipality. We wanted them to give their opinions, to pronounce themselves with regard to this indictment. And it was not our intention, but I also believe that we sent a letter to Mr. Cassese, who at that time was the President of the Tribunal at that time. So all these letters were written with only one goal in mind, "Please collect evidence, and after you've collected evidence, we shall come. It will suffice for you to call us by telephone or in any other way, and we shall come by ourselves. There is no need to arrest us, to follow us, to wound us, or do whatever. We're ready to come. We're offering to put up some guarantees, from money to depositing our passports or whatever, but we're about ready to come here." Perhaps we were naive, but that was how we thought and in what way our minds worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Right. At the time when you wrote those letters, and that was mid-1997, were you all in Vitez at the time, I mean people who signed those letters, or were they all in hiding? Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you. Those who were in Vitez were in hiding. The only one who was not in Vitez was Mr. Vlado Santic. He was not living there at the time, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After you sent those letters, was there any feedback? How were those letters received? What was going on? Anything about your status?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, no, there was not any direct feedback, but I believe those letters helped, even if indirectly, to set in motion -- I think it was done at a very high level -- to set in motion all the preparations for our voluntary surrender, and it happened on the 6th of October, '97. I think that those letters were the ones which paved the way to all the other events, and we know the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After that, did you leave Vitez or did you stay in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was done the latter half of '97, and the elections were forthcoming, and I thought it would be very dangerous to stay in Vitez because there would be many people coming in to observe those elections, and I was also guessing that some other people might be coming who might either be trying to come by some information or do certain other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I left Vitez then and was not there for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is, you went into hiding. Do you know where Mirjan or Zoran Kupreskic were at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: They had stayed behind. They were in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Katava. Mr. Usher, will you please show these documents to the witness and, of course, to the Chamber. These are the letters Mr. Katava mentioned a moment ago and which were already adduced under D47/2. But at that time, they were not admitted because at that time the translations were missing, I mean English translations were missing. I should like to adduce them, to tender them into evidence now, and I should like to ask Mr. Katava to confirm their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac, please. Microphone for Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac. We could not hear the beginning of the question. We're sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the author of this? Was it Mr. Zvonimir Cilic on the 11th of May, '97? This is the first letter, isn't it? Could they be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first letter is addressed to -- yes, we should show it. This was the first letter. This was the first letter, and then a broader version, an expanded version, was written. Mr. Cilic read it in front of Mr. Steiner and handed it over to him. Let me just say that all the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time covered this and transmitted the substance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Other letters were written by you in cooperation with co-signatories?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not quite. Let's say that we all drew them up, wrote them and initialled in full consensus. I think that means something. I repeat, Mr. Vlado Santic was not there. He was the only one who did not take part in this, even though we did communicate by telephone and discuss it. But this was the joint effort.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you can confirm that all those letters were the product of your joint initiative and your joint effort at the time; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Will you tell us just one more thing? Yesterday you said that you were sorry that you had not struck a friendship -- you had not stricken a friendship with Mr. Zoran Kupreskic earlier. Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I really was sorry about that, because as a young man, when I was 17 or 18, I used to be a member of a folk dancing group in Vukovar, and I'm sorry that in perhaps 1977, when I moved into Vitez, I did not join such a nice cultural society, the protagonists of which were the brothers Kupreskic. That is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should now like to adduce into evidence D47/2, that it be now admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be D108/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, D48/2. You did say "48"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this is in your numbering, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. D108.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection. Thank you. All right. It is admitted into evidence as D108/2. As you know, today we will have to adjourn at 1.00. I would like to suggest that we go on until quarter to 11.00 and then we have a 30-minute break, only one break. So if you don't mind, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. Mr. Katava, good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: My name is Michael Blaxill, and I'm one of the prosecuting counsel in this case. As a result of your testimony yesterday and today, I do have a few questions I would like to ask you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just to clarify one point you mentioned yesterday, there was another Mr. Marinko Katava you referred to from Busovaca. You referred to that person being younger than yourself. Could you indicate how old that person was, say in 1993, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yesterday, perhaps you did not hear it from the interpreters. Yesterday, I said that that bloke, that person, was born when I was serving in the army, and that was 1971, so it could have been '71 or perhaps '72. Early '72 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you worked in a large commercial enterprise, as a senior executive in Impregnacija, in 1992; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: '92, yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you just indicate, sir, the local municipality authority that had the effective power and control in the Vitez and Lasva Valley region in late 1992, that is, around October? Was that in fact the authority of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, was that the effective power?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm afraid that you might draw me into political waters, and I really don't swim particularly well in that kind of waters, who was the authority. In 1990, I was a member of the municipal electoral commission. That was the first time we were having multi-party elections in Vitez. After those elections, there was another round of elections, and I was removed, I was removed from that commission, and I suppose my only sin was I was not a member of the HDZ. So as far as the politics is concerned, I was trying hard not to step into it with one foot, I mean let alone both my feet. Now, I know, of course, a lot of time has passed by, and one thinks back. Of course, the results of the multi-party elections were, as we know, unfavourable for Muslims, who were somewhat few in numbers. Croats should have had the majority in the parliament, and I don't know -- I really don't know what happened. But they set up their parallel bodies of authority and so on and so forth, and then it followed an undesirable course and ended as it ended, in what it shouldn't have ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, I'm not trying to draw you into political opinions of any sort. What I'm asking you is as a businessman in a large company, you have to function presumably with things like permits and various things with local authorities. To the best of your recall, was it correct that it was that authority, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or the HVO, was that the effective authority that you had to deal with and that people had to deal with in the course of business?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The only person communicating with the authorities was the general manager. I could communicate only with at that time it was called the employment fund, when we needed some more employed or when things relative to social security had to be done. That was the former foundation for social insurance. And there were people who had been working there for years before that, and people that I communicated with, that I maintained contact with, were the same before and after the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Katava, we can move on from there. You say you were a member of the hunting society. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How many members did the hunting society have, do you recall, in, let us say, late 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Around 300, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You made reference in your evidence yesterday that during the conflict with, I think, the Serb aggression as you referred to it, your members of your hunting group were, in fact, deployed in some way on a protective line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was not the protective line, and there was no direct contact with -- I don't know what term you use here -- with Serbs. Let it be, shall we say, in quotation marks. I mean that was the terminology we used. There was no direct contact with them. But there is visibility from Vlasic where the Yugoslav forces were deployed, there is a very good view of this whole area or the picnic area that we used at Zabrdze and to Poljane. There was a very good view of this. So why did we go up there? To protect that part of the hunting grounds and to let the Serbs see that that area was covered, so as to try to dissuade them from any possible idea or attempt at an assault, perhaps an attempt to take over the Impregnacija plant. That was the idea. So we -- or perhaps, I mean, being as hunters, you know, hunters, that is a very good opportunity for us to spend seven days together, socialising, having a couple of drinks, perhaps having somebody say something, roasting some game, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, Mr. Katava, this was some kind of social event, or were there to protect territory from the, quote, "Serb aggressors"?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "social event". It was not a party, it was not a party, but we did have a good time there. But we also thought that we were useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you at any time become involved in any kind of active combat activity with Serb forces in that location?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, there was no contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It's true to say, however, that there was active combat between Serb forces and other forces, including predominantly Croat forces, in that region at that time; is that not so? There was a war going on, wasn't there, of sorts?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there was a war. However, that was away from our lines. That was -- we were overlooking the city, the town of Vitez, and the fighting was above Novi Travnik and on Mount Vlasic. That was the line. The position was called something like Kamenjar or Kamenjas where both units of both sides were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, I presume you were armed at the time when you were doing that duty. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I assume you were wearing your hunting kit or some kind of outdoor clothing, or was it possibly parts of uniforms, when you were performing those functions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I talked about the weapons I had yesterday. I had those weapons with me then, and I still have them at home today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How many times did you go out to that area and perform this duty and whatever else took place?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was in the second half of 1992. I explained yesterday that every fourth week, we went for seven days to Zabrdze.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The members or presumably the numbers of a group that would go out there, how were they chosen and how were they notified of their turn to do that duty?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Our head huntsman drew up a roster and he read it out once, and then all the hunters knew, because of that roster, when their turn was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Are you aware as to whether the head hunter or any other member of that society had contact with HVO military people to coordinate what you did with whatever other defences were in place?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty, but I assume they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We'll move on, if we may, sir, to the 20th of October, 1992. There was a certain event that's been often referred to here as the first conflict in Ahmici. Were you aware of that event in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move forward, if I may, sir, to the 15th of April of 1993. You stated yesterday that as far as you were concerned, this was a normal working day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That you retired to bed after the 10.00 news?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And that you slept through until, I believe you said, about 05.30 hours on the 16th, when detonations awoke you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You made reference at that point where people said they got up, maybe washed, maybe dressed, whichever order. Do you recall what you did and about what time it was that you left your apartment to go outside the building?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can only repeat what I said yesterday. We were awakened in a hurry. The first thing I did was to look after my children -- they were crying and they were sleepy -- and to put them in the corridor where I felt they were safest. I don't remember whether I washed, but I certainly dressed, and then I went downstairs to the entrance of the building. All this could have taken 10 or 15 minutes, so it must have been between half past 5.00 and 6.00 or a quarter past 6.00. However, I did not look at my watch. No one did then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you got outside your building, you encountered and/or were joined by a number of your neighbours, and all of those were Croat neighbours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In the beginning, as I said yesterday, Mr. Stojkovici, Mr. Stipo Krizanac, were already there when I arrived, and I think that Marijan Vinac was there. But there were seven or eight people whom I listed, and they were there. They came and went, and this went on for five, six or seven days. That was the time we spent at the entrance to the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I can just stick at this point in time, sir, to the 16th of April of 1993, I believe you said yesterday that none of your Muslim or indeed Serb neighbours came out of their apartments, and yet a number of your Croat neighbours did. I believe you said that, sir. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's not what I said, that's not what I said. I will repeat what I said yesterday. Milisav Bacanovic, my neighbour, is a Montenegrin, my neighbour Stojkovici from A6 is a Serb, and they were, I think, there throughout this whole time with us. The Muslim neighbours, during that day, did come from time to time. I mentioned Mr. Salkic from the first floor. He came and offered us cigarettes, something to drink. Another neighbour, Mirsad, I mentioned his name yesterday. (redacted) would come. We went to have coffee with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you were outside on the street, did you see any other persons, and in particular did you see any military personnel on the street?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were not in the street. We were at the entrance into the building, which has some stairs leading up and there's a small corridor, and we would run over the four big stairs and we would -- we were actually underneath the staircase for protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But presumably from the entranceway, there were times that you were able to look into the street; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: There is no street, there's just a side street passing by, and at that time there was not much traffic even on the normal days. All we could see was the big parking lot in front of this building and the other buildings which enclosed our view. There are four other buildings in front of ours and then the road is behind them, so we were unable to see what was going on. But as I said, that part of town was deserted. It was like a ghost town in those days. There were not even any stray dogs in the street because their instinct probably told them to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So if I may encapsulate what you're saying, sir, are you telling us that you did not at any time see any soldiers outside your building during the 16th of April, 1993, or did you see any kind of soldiers outside your building during that day? That's, I hope, simple enough, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that on the 16th of April, if that is the day we are talking about, I think there was no movement. If you asked me about soldiers, I assume we are referring to units, no, there were no military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will ask just one more question relating to that specific issue, Mr. Katava, and that is this: Did you see any single soldiers in the vicinity of your building that day, not military units but men in uniform carrying weapons? Did you see anybody like that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think there were people who came and went. They were individuals, and it wasn't often, and there were not many of them. I don't know about that first day, whether anybody came or went, but in the following four or five days, there were people who came and went and who were in uniform. But they were always individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now be asking to move into private session for a very short period of time. Bearing in mind it's a quarter to, it might be a good idea to recommence in that private session and take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Katava, you stated that on the morning of the 16th -- and I've taken a couple of quotations from your testimony yesterday -- you said that you wanted to protect your neighbours. And then you said, " ... and what we had heard was really bad." And you also made the expression, " ... to forestall or prevent anyone's bad conduct." Now, what bad conduct were you expecting or afraid of that required to you protect your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said yesterday that we wanted first of all to protect our families, our children, and I said that from what had already happened, we could not expect anything good. We wanted to protect them from something we did not know. We did not know what might happen the next minute, the next hour, the next day, and we didn't know that for the whole time, 350 days that the town was surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, I'm asking you simply on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993, and you have stated in evidence here that you wanted to protect your neighbours. You also said that, quote, "What we had heard was really bad." Now, let's start with that: What had you heard that you say was, quote, "really bad"?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The detonations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you're saying at this point in time, your concern was for your neighbours because there were shells falling nearby; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Please, I would like to repeat, I was worried most of all about my family and only then about my neighbours and all the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But if your concern was for the results of shells falling, presumably possibly falling on your building, presumably the interests of protection applied equally to all of you; what could you do to help your neighbours from falling shells?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: You are putting words in my mouth. Fortunately, shells were not falling on my building, or as far as I could see, around it. They were not falling. However, who could say that the next one would not fall on my van or into the entranceway or into my apartment or somebody else's apartment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So in that way, in what manner did you think you could offer protection to your neighbours by visiting their apartments? How would that offer any assistance if a shell fell on that building?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: What am I supposed to answer to such a question? It is difficult even to think back and remember 1993. How can one protect anyone from shells falling? Well, there is no way. There is no protection from that. But how one can help, to perhaps help that the consequences are less fateful, what kind of help? Well, I just thought that we were there and that we perhaps could help somehow. How, I don't know, because nothing like that happened. But had something happened, had somebody been wounded or injured or whatever, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Subsequently, then, what prompted your comment -- and I believe I've noted this accurately from yesterday -- you wanted to forestall or prevent anyone's bad conduct? Let's move on from shelling. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you want me once again to use the noun "threat." But if the explosions were as horrible as that, if there were bursts of gunfire, then that particular noun can mean only something unknown. To protect: How? We could not really know who could be coming, with what intent. I'm not going back to history, but say you have an earthquake and the thieves see an opportunity to do their job, so in a situation such as it was, criminals -- and you find them everywhere; if nothing else, we would be preventing robberies, theft, burglaries, say. Theft, robbery, things like that. Whether we could prevent something else, I don't really know what, and with what, if you wish. But we were there, and we are talking about five, six, or seven men who are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will put it to you, Mr. Katava, and you can agree or disagree as you see fit: Weren't you really concerned as to the potential conduct of HVO soldiers towards some of the occupants of your apartment block? Would that be fair to say, on my part, or not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: In all that was unknown, in what I call the unknown, one part -- but perhaps only one part -- of that unknown might have been a threat of that kind. And why not the other way around? Why not the other way around, too? So the other way around is, again, only one part of that unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, do you recall what happened the following day, the 17th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I think it was similar to that one. As a matter of fact, all the days were -- every day was like the day before it or the day after it. I can't really single out that particular day for any reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall when, possibly, whether or not you saw any military people in the course of that day or perhaps the following day, the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just before we had the break, I said that on the 16th, that I think that on the 16th, nobody came or went. I'm referring to men in uniform; I'm referring to uniformed people. On the 17th or on the 18th, I think -- not, however, to my entrance, but I think to other entrances which we could see, I think that men came -- or rather entered and went out, and we assumed that they were the tenants, the residents of those particular entrances. And they were always individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason, sir, why the entrance to your apartments did not attract the attention of soldiers, whereas clearly you say they visited other entrances to apartments in the immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I can't -- I just can't give any definite answer why was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe, sir, some days later you say that you were actually, yourself, mobilised into the HVO forces -- is that correct? -- somewhere after the 20th? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You've indicated to this Court that you knew Mr. Vlado Santic for a period of some 15 to 17 years. That is correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and I described the relations between us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you knew what his profession was, that he was a civilian police officer; did you later become aware of any change of profession, to military police or an HVO role played by Mr. Santic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did not meet often.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So if I were to suggest to you, sir, that at April, 1993, Mr. Vlado Santic was a military police officer, would you able to say, "Yes, that is within my knowledge," or "No, I don't know that"?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, at that time, I did not know where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you have any or much contact with Mr. Vlado Santic in late 1992, prior to the conflict breaking out?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Let me repeat what I have already said. Whenever we met, and that was always by chance, we would greet one another in the street, and that was all. That was the kind of acquaintanceship between us. We never even had, say, coffee together in a cafe, or whatever. Nothing like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In the latter stages, when you might have encountered Mr. Santic on the street, did you ever see him wearing uniform?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: When? Later when?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Late 1992, or in the early months of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I never saw him. If we are talking about the end of 1992, I did not see him. I did not see him one single time during the war. I was deployed at a completely different place, and I do not know where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I may just have the Court's indulgence for a moment, Your Honours. I'm advised, Your Honour, that concludes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, you confirmed today that you were mobilised on the 20th of April, 1993, and a while ago you said that you were assigned to a completely different duty and that you did not know where Vlado Santic was. Could you tell us, where was it that you had been assigned to?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it seems that I am the only one here who is trying to be accurate. Where could I be? I said that I was assigned between the 20th and the 22nd, and I asked you to leave that particular period of time, time frame, not on the 20th but between the 20th and the 22nd. A courier from the Defence office served the paper, the assignment. I wouldn't call it the engineering unit, I would call it a unit made of a very small number of men who had the skill and the knowledge how to provide alternative routes to Nova Bila, that is, the alternative route to Busovaca, as the main road was under fire, let me put it that way, under gunfire, so that we were using some paths, some lanes, some forest paths which we filled, which we broadened, in order to provide conditions for the transport of the wounded in the direction of Novi Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, will you tell me, until that 20th or the 21st of April, '93, did you have an army uniform?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time, did you have any personal army weapon?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Army weapon, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know how to use an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You were asked today about those detonations, about those explosions, and you told us something about that. Could you tell me if you had any advance knowledge of any explosion?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that you wanted to protect the neighbours in your building, did you mean all your neighbours, both of the Croat and Muslim ethnicity or any other ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never distinguished people by religion or ethnic origin or the colour of their skin, and I wish all people would just distinguish people as people, as those who are human and those who are not, and if you ask me today, I would do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were afraid of something unknown and that that was why, at your entrance, you organised for this whole residential block a kind of security. You said, of course, that you wouldn't be able to prevent a shell falling or anticipate where it would fall, but could you say that the warnings -- that what you did for your neighbours were just some kind of instructions, some kind of advice as to how to protect themselves at that particular moment?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: How much we hoped to contribute to helping them, to protect them, we meant of course women and children, we were trying to tell them how to protect them to try to calm them down. How successful we were, of course, is very difficult to tell. But fortunately, I must say, fortunately there were no effects, there were no consequences; that is, these people, life and limbs of those people were not in danger. I don't know when that particular explosion happened. That was when, of course, all the window panes broke, and then we went around and looked for some plastic, for some clips or for whatever to protect those windows. We were going around and looking for paper clips to fix those things, so that was this natural help, and I think that it is just normal, natural, neighbourly assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend for the Prosecution asked you if that threat from somebody unknown included also the threat coming from the HVO, and in your reply, you allowed such a possibility, of course if I understood you well. Will you tell me if one of such possible threats would also include threats from individuals, from supporters, or from groups related in some way to the BH army; was that possible?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course, that is what I said, and that was only part of that unknown, and also the reverse could also play a part in that unknown. So I am repeating. At my entrance with 12 apartments, if you are forcing me to distinguish people, to give out people, there were four Croats in those 12 apartments. But of course we could have had the reverse situation, that a Croat also could have been under threat. That was also an unknown then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So if I'm understanding you properly, you thought that all the people were vulnerable, that the threat could be coming from anyone, from robbers, burglars, and so on and so forth. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go, just for a moment, into private session, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open session) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mrs. Veronique Fonville, good morning. Could you please make the solemn declaration as an interpreter? First the interpreter and then the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will do so faithfully, independently, impartially, and with full respect for the duty of confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, this is as an interpreter. And now the solemn declaration of Mrs. Hume, Johanna Hume, as a witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated, and I will ask Counsel Pavkovic to start with the examination in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: This is in open session. I'm just checking. May we begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, madam. We talked, or rather you talked to our legal assistant, Mr. Vrdoljak, and he explained to you the reasons for which we wanted to ask you to come here and give your evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I have to introduce myself. I'm Petar Pavkovic, and I am the Defence counsel for Vladimir Santic, and I will ask you some questions today about subjects which you have already been informed about. You know what we shall like to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I hope we shall be able to overcome linguistic difficulties and others. If you have any question or if you have any suggestions, of course, I shall be quite happy to help you. So madam, please, will you tell us your name? Tell us your name, your full name, the date of your birth, and where do you live, the place of residence.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: My name is Johanna Hume, and -- shall I answer in English or in Dutch?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In English, if you have a command of English. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Okay. I'm born the 23rd of April, 1960, in Amsterdam, and I live in Amsterdam now at this day. It's difficult for me, because I hear the Croatian language and I understand it, and I have to listen to this lady who translates it. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Would you tune in to channel 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's channel 4. Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you hear English now? Can you hear English?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, I can, but I also understand the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Even better.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, we realise you can understand us all perfectly, and we can all understand you. So will you please give us, once again, your full name, the year of your birth, and your address?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: My full name is Johanna Henriette Hume, and I'm born the 23rd of April, 1960, in Amsterdam, and I live now Amsteldijk 97 in Amsterdam.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This perhaps is a personal question, but I must ask you because it is important for me. Are you married?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: No, I'm not married.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, I've been married.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you are divorced, are you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, I'm divorced. I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you change your name after your divorce?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What was your former surname?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: The name of my husband, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: That was Dasovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you tell me if you have any children?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, I have two children, two daughters called Ana and Branka Dasovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 or, rather, 1993, how old were your children?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Six or seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: [Inaudible]... was about nine, ten years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, did your older daughter, that is, the elder daughter Ana, go to school? I'm referring to the '92/'93 school year.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes. Both my daughters went to the same school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps if, on a certain occasion, your daughter told you something, and you found it important, that a new pupil had joined her class?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: In December 1992, a new child, a girl, came to Ana's class, and she was from Bosnia. She came from Bosnia and she joined the class, and I told the teacher that if there were any problems with the language, it was possible for me to translate from Bosnian to Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what happened then and what the name of the little girl was?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: I went to the school, and my daughter Ana said, "This is the girl," and she told me her name was Ema Alilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, did you become acquainted with her father?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes. I told her, in the hall of the school, in the Croatian language, "I'm the mother of Ana, and if your parents need any help and they don't speak the language, I can help you." She told her parents that, and after that I -- the same afternoon, her mother came to my house and invited me to come and meet the whole family, and that included her father.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what her mother's name was?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: The name of the mother is Dragica Krizanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Her name is Dragica Krizanac now, but it was Dragica Alilovic then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, did you visit the Alilovic family?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, several times. Almost every week, I came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We are at the beginning. I will ask you about that later on. Could you tell me, when did you visit the Alilovic family for the first time? Was it in late 1992, early 1993; can you remember at all? Do you recall a certain day or a certain occasion, apart from the time you came to meet the family, as you told us just a while ago?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: I met -- I went to the home the first time in December 1992. I don't know the exact date, but it must be between Sinterklaas, that's the 5th of December, and Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Today, madam, you told us that you understand the Croatian language or the Bosnian language. Did you talk to them in the Bosnian language then?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes. To the parents, to Stipo and Dragica, I only spoke Croatian, because he didn't understand one word of Dutch; maybe "thank you" or "hello", but that was all. So I spoke only Croatian with the parents, Dragica and Stipo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how old their children were then and how many children they had?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: They have two children, and Ema was the same age as my oldest daughter, about ten years old. She's half a year younger than my daughter. Her birthday is in June, and my daughter's birthday is in December. And they have a son, Petar, and Petar's birthday I don't know, but he was seven years younger than his sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When you talk about Ema, you're talking about Emilija, in fact?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Emilija, but her name in Holland was Ema because "Emilija" was too -- she said she wished to prefer her name is Ema, and because one of our queens was called Ema, she was very proud to use that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you lived in the vicinity, you were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes. We weren't direct neighbours, but they lived now two minutes walking, at the most, from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So your children went to the same school?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the teacher's name was at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Christine. She was called Christine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the principal of the school was at that time? What was the name of the gentleman who was the school principal then?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: The school principal was called Wout Groenwald or Groenwoud. I don't remember exactly, but it is Groenwald or Groenwoud, and his first name is Wout.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell me a little about the customs prevailing today -- and I presume they did then, in 1992, 1993 -- because you yourself are also a teacher. Did parents, especially parents of young children, have to bring their children to school and come to collect them after the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Can you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: My question is the following: Do parents have to accompany their children to school and come to collect them when classes are over?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes. That's common in Holland, that you bring your children to school and that you collect them in the afternoon, and then you bring them back for the afternoon school, and then you collect them at 15 past 3.00. And -- well, there are some mothers who don't bring their children, but I brought my children every day to school, and I would collect them at the end of the day, till they were 10, 11 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: If we recall that time now, 1992, 1993, can you tell us whether the Alilovic family also did this and accompanied their children to school and came to collect them?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes. Most times, the father, Stipo Alilovic, came to school. He waited at the fence. There was the street, with a fence, and he waited there and smoked a cigarette, and he waited there for his children till they came out. He never entered the school. There were also mothers who entered the school, but he never did. He always waited outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you used to see him?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Almost every day, yeah, but also in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you used to see him, and you would probably talk to him when you met him in front of the school?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We didn't have big conversations every day, but I always greeted him and said, "How are you," and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you used to see him at his house as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Sometimes the children played together, and we went there for coffee or for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
