utterances.text: As far as we know so far, their son, Petar, the son of Stipo and Dragica Alilovic, was young at that time. He went to kindergarten. Do you know anything about who took him there and when, and what is usually done in respect of this?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Well, the younger son, I know at the mornings, the oldest -- Ema took him for school. In Holland, it's the custom that children go to school from four years old. So when they are four years old, they go to school. But at the same school, that's called a primary school, there's also the peuterspeelzaal. I don't know the English word, but it's called "peuterspeelzaal." It's a play school for little children, and it's in the same building. He went there first, for a year, until he was four years old, and then he went to the first class of primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that he was taken by someone; who took him, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: In the mornings his older sister took him, so Ema took him, and in the afternoons, his father or his mother would collect him. But mostly Stipo collected the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You knew from your conversations with him that Stipo and Dragica Alilovic had arrived as refugees from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us today that you offered to help them, and that you did?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you help them put their documents in order, the documents concerning their refugee status?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we go on, or would you like to take a break? How do you feel? You can tell us.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: I am all right now. I just have to concentrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you helped the Alilovic family in their everyday worries and concerns about their refugee status; can you please tell us something about this?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Well, they didn't have status when I met them for the first time. They were without status. They had to have been several months in a refugee camp, in "Asielzoekerscentrum," we called it, here in the Netherlands. But they have got a ROA house, that's a house where refugees without status can live for several time, so they don't have to be in a camp, because it's very stressing. And when I met him, the whole family didn't have status; but in May, 1993, the family got status and went together to the vreemdelingenpolitie, a foreign police, the -- I don't know how it's called, vreemdelingenpolitie, in the Bijlmermeer in Amsterdam, and there the whole family got their "A" status. "A" is the best status you can get here as a refugee. Then you can get your family here, and you have the same rights as Dutch people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in May 1993, they achieved this refugee status; up to that time, did they have any documents to prove their identity? Did they have any documents at all, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: They had -- when you get your "A" status, you all get a document where it's printed on -- I don't know how it looks like, but -- and you can ask, if you don't have your own passport, you can ask here for a vluchtelingenpaspoort, a refugee passport. I don't know where they have -- I know they had some kind of identification, but I don't know exactly what. They all had papers from the foreign police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: During this time, while someone is waiting to get their refugee status, regardless of what you said about seeing Stipo almost every day, was it possible to leave your place of residence, or did you have to go to the police and report the to police on a regular basis to show that you were here?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: You can leave your place of residence; that's possible. You can't leave the country, because you don't have a passport. When Stipo and Dragica asked for permission to stay here, they had to give their passports to the police. They can travel in our country freely. When they lived in the refugee camp, the Asielzoekerscentrum, you have to go there every week and get -- you get a stamp. But when you live in a ROA house, that isn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that up to May 1993, Stipo Alilovic did not have a passport? He could not have left the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: No, never, he could have not -- no, that's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you tell me, madam, do you know that Stipo Alilovic has died?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Stipo Alilovic died?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: 25 October, 1995. I saw him about one hour after he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: From what you have told us, it is evident that you were on good terms with the Alilovic family and that you were, one might say, friends. I assume that you knew about many of their little secrets, as people usually find these out when they associate as friends. Can you tell me, did the Alilovic family during that time have money?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Money? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How did they live?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: They didn't have money. They -- they came from a refugee camp, and they lived in a ROA house. That means that the central organisation for refugees paid the rent and paid for electricity and gas, and they received, I think, monthly, the whole family, 800 guilders to buy their clothes, to buy their food, to buy the necessary things. And when they hadn't status, they didn't receive child support. We know -- child support, "kinderbijslag" it's called in Dutch. But when you have no status, you don't -- you don't have a right for that money. They received it not until they had their "A" status. So it was -- yeah, bad for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So they could meet only their minimum needs?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And when associating with the Alilovic family, you were probably able to discuss -- and I assume you did -- these things, so you probably were able to learn the attitude Stipo Alilovic had toward the war that was then going on in Bosnia. Do you remember having such conversations with him?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Well, we talked about the war in Bosnia, because a lot of family of both Dragica and Stipo still lived there. He hated the war. He didn't want to talk about it very much, because he always said, "I don't understand why there is war there, why our neighbours have to be like that to each other." And he told me why he was here in the Netherlands, because he received a letter from the Croatian army that he had to appear for his military duties, and at that moment he escaped. He went to his sister in Austria and from there to Holland, because he didn't want to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam, can you describe in greater detail the physical appearance of Stipo Alilovic?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Well, the physical appearance, many children in our neighbourhood were terribly afraid of him because he had a big, black beard, a big moustache, and he looked a bit -- and he had hair on his nose. It grew from his nose. You don't see it often, but he had it. He looked a bit -- yeah, angry, but he wasn't. But many children, when they saw him, they -- they run.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would now like to ask that the witness be shown a document, C10. That is a document with a photograph of Stipo Alilovic, so that the witness can look at it and say whether it is Stipo Alilovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us what that exhibit number is? Because C10 doesn't match with a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: We have C10 and C11. C10 is a card, a bank card.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, I would now like to ask you to look at this photograph and to tell us whether this photograph shows Stipo Alilovic, the person we have been talking about today.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes. This is him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you absolutely sure this is him?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, from what we have said today, may we conclude that not a day or two had passed without your seeing Stipo Alilovic from the time of his arrival in the Netherlands up to his death in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes. From the time -- it's not completely correct; I saw him from the day he came in Amsterdam till the day of his death. I didn't meet the family when they were in the refugee camp. I met them in December '92, when they came to Amsterdam.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would now like to go into private session, because I would like

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Private session, please. Thank you. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I shall repeat my question, madam. Could you tell us how you came to learn Croatian?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: I married on the 6th of a August, 1980, with a man who is called Dasovic. He lived in Zdencina, a small village 20 kilometres from Zagreb. I met him here in Holland, and we married. His parents didn't speak one word of Dutch or German or English, or anybody in that village spoke another language, so I thought, when I have to communicate with the people who are now my family and the friends of my husband, I have to learn Croatian language. So I went here to -- in Amsterdam you have the Volksuniversiteit, and there I took two years of course in Croatian language. That was after the first time I went there. And I spoke with my parents-in-law and with friends of my husband's also with a dictionary. I learn quickly languages. That's my advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't doubt that. How long did you live in Croatia, as such? Could you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: I never lived in Croatia. I went there for -- we lived in Amsterdam. My former husband still lives in Amsterdam. But we went there for holidays. We went there for six weeks every summer to visit the family of my husband: his father, his mother, sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, do you have any special skills as to the foreign police, as to bylaws on cross-border traffic, on travels by refugees, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I don't know in detail every single rule, but I know that -- I know about status, and I know a "C," and "E," and "A," and -- I know how it works. And I was married to a foreigner, too, so -- and he did have -- yeah, it's called "C," because he was married to a Dutch woman. And I -- yeah, I worked with refugees. I gave Dutch as second language to refugees who lived in Bussum. So I also heard there from the rules that exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: In the Netherlands, as is the case in other European countries, do you have associations which are designed to help refugees?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes. In Holland, Vluchtelingenwerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, are you a member of an association or several associations?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: [Inaudible] You get help from there. When you are a refugee, you go there and you ask help, but you can be a member of any kind of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I shall repeat my question in a different way; I don't think we understood each other. Speaking about these associations helping refugees, to do so they use nationals, don't they, Dutch people?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you employed by one such association?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: I haven't been.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's speak about the children and their schooling. You told us that in the Netherlands, it is customary for one or either of the parents to go and collect the children from school. However, from what you told us, it seems as though children went on their own to school in the morning, by themselves.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: No, not every child is going alone, but when they are small, small, until six, eight, ten years old, it's also depending on the distance you live from the school. Amsterdam is a big, busy city, and you can take your children along when they are small. So you have to bring your children every day to school, but there are children who are brought by an older sister or older brother who is also visiting the same school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let us speak about the Alilovic family. I believe I heard earlier on from you that as far as you could remember, Ema would take her small brother to the school in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes she took her brother in the morning when her mother wasn't ready to go, or the father.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So it would happen that the children would go by themselves to school?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes, but it's different between me and the family Alilovic, because when I pointed out the school of our children was here -- yeah, I don't know how to point it out. Here they lived. They lived about 20, 30 metres from the school, and I lived a few streets further.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So would the children sometimes go home alone, by themselves?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: No, never, only when Mr. Alilovic got ill later on, they sometimes went alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Is there any special reason why the children could go alone to school but couldn't come back by themselves? Was there any special reason for that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: No, but -- they sometimes went alone to school, and not every day. Most of the times, the mother or the father brought, and only when one of the parents couldn't come, they went alone. I don't know the exact reason. I also -- I know that Mr. Alilovic liked to get his children from school, and also she liked to get them from school, because they could talk with the neighbours and talk with the teacher, and it was not only necessary but also social.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I can understand that perfectly. However, this is my question: You said that it would sometimes happen that the two children would go to school by themselves without being accompanied. Hence my question. Would it also sometimes happen that they would go home from school by themselves?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So it would happen that parents, either the mother or the father, did not get their children from school, that that would sometimes happen; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You also testified that sometimes the mother would go and collect the kids from school, so you cannot say that you would see the father of those children every day?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Well, the mother -- Dragica Alilovic, she went to school. When they got their status, our status, in Amsterdam you can follow school, so she went to school from that time on to learn the Dutch language. But he didn't want that because he wasn't interested in that, and he stayed at the house with the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's speak about the period going from December '92 to April '93, so this is the period we are interested in. At that time, do you remember that it was the mother who would sometimes pick up the kids from school?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's speak about the financial means of that family, as you assessed them. Between December of '92 and April of '93, did either or both of the parents work?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: You cannot work here when you are waiting for your status.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll put the question differently. Did one or the other of the parents, for that period going from December '92 to April '93, did either of them have any professional activity of kinds?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Krizanac recognised and admitted that at the time, not that she would have a professional activity because she was sort of not allowed to, but she would work in a restaurant. Did you know that information?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: She worked in a restaurant in Bloemendaal. That's a village near Amsterdam. She worked there in the kitchen, but that is not a regular job. That was illegal. We call it black, black work, because she didn't pay taxes. She wasn't allowed to work, and the family was really in big financial trouble. And I know also the people where she worked, I know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find her that job?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I don't know exactly who, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: It is just by chance that you happened to know both people?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yeah. The owner of that restaurant is a friend of my former husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you mention that activity when such questions were raised?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Because it wasn't allowed. When it's public that she worked without permission, she would have to pay it back, still now when they find out that she worked illegal. How should I say it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure I speak on behalf of the Judges when I tell you that this Tribunal is not going to bother Mrs. Krizanac. She's not going to be disturbed at all. Did Mr. Alilovic have another type of work of the same kind?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Only later he did, when he got his papers. August of '93, he played in a movie in Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Alilovic family have a car?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: They bought it in June or July, right after they had status. They got their status in May, and shortly after that they bought I think an Opel, Opel Kadett, a green one. I drove it when Mr. Alilovic was seen in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean that prior to April 1993, they didn't have a car?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. or Mrs. Alilovic speak to you about what had happened in April '93 in Central Bosnia, in the Lasva River Valley? Did you hear about this from them?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: No. Yeah, we saw it on television, what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. or Mrs. Alilovic comment on what had happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: She asked me -- he asked me, "Did you see it?" "Yes, I did." And he said, "That's the place where I was born. That's the surroundings where I was born."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know one of his cousins? I think he was Tomislav Alilovic.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: He lives in Holland; is that correct? No. I think that he has family here in Holland, but I don't remember they are from her side or his side, I don't know, and I don't know the exact names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know a cousin of his named Tomislav; do you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: I can't recall. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you if you know him personally or not. That's easy to answer. Tomislav.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: I know people called Tomislav, but not in that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned Tomislav Alilovic, cousin of Stipo, and he too was born in Ahmici in Central Bosnia, and that doesn't ring any bell?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: No. I know the family of Stipo, but I don't know their names, I don't recall their names. I know there lived a nephew in Germany, but I don't know their names. I saw them at the funeral of Mr. Alilovic. Then I saw them all, but I don't know which one is Tomislav or which one has another name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do not have any more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have a very minor question, madam. I wonder whether you could clarify a matter as a proper question of curiosity. It struck me that this document, the Dutch document relating to your appointment as a secondary school teacher, has the date of the 6th of July, '93. However, it relates to an appointment to be made as from the 16th of April, '93. How is it that it was taken almost three months after the actual appointment?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNA HUME
utterances.text: Yeah, that's common in Holland, because you get an appointment or you get your -- you are employed as a teacher but the school is a part of the City Council, but the administrative handlings, they come always later. That's very normal in school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Thank you so much. All right. I think there are no other questions. Thank you, madam, for testifying today, thank you so much indeed. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In five minutes, we will adjourn. But before doing so, may I ask Counsel Pavkovic about the list of witnesses for tomorrow? Just one witness, only one?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, tomorrow we have only Andjelko Alilovic scheduled because a witness refused and said she did not want to give evidence here. We learned about that on the 1st of this month, after we had submitted the timetable for our witnesses, and that is why we had to go through it and change it once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I was wondering whether one of the witnesses for the 8th of July could also be ready for tomorrow, just in case we get through with Mr. Vidovic, so that we can have a reserve witness, one of the three, for Thursday, if they are around in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: They will be arriving tonight sometime after 9.00, or perhaps 10.00 tonight. Of course, we had to take note of the expenses, and so the witnesses arrive on the eve of. They will be coming as envisaged by the original schedule, so they will be here late tonight, and I'm really not sure whether they would be up to appearing in the court tomorrow. But of course we shall bear that in mind, and we shall be seeing them tonight, and if any one of them feels really strong, well enough to appear tomorrow, then of course we shall inform you about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's make an effort. So we will adjourn now until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
